<!-- WHAT THIS PAGE IS FOR
     Case studies are the bridge between the research page and the
     partnerships page. A business reader will not open a journal article, but
     will read two pages about a problem that looks like theirs.

     Write each one to a fixed shape: the situation, what you did, what
     changed. Resist the urge to lead with method — practitioners care about
     the problem and the outcome, and will trust the method if the outcome
     holds up.

     BEFORE PUBLISHING ANY CASE STUDY INVOLVING A REAL ORGANIZATION:
       - Get written permission to name them, or anonymize ("a mid-size
         regional manufacturer"). Verbal agreement is not enough.
       - Check your IRB determination if the work involved human subjects.
         Research findings and a public write-up are different disclosures.
       - Do not include client data, even aggregated, without explicit sign-off.
       - Student-collaborative work: get the student's permission and credit
         them by name. FERPA aside, it is theirs too.

     Anonymized case studies work fine for credibility. Named ones work better,
     but only get one of those by asking. -->
